strengths: Principled perspective on grokking: The paper provides a clean, intuitive explanation linking the delayed generalization plateau in grokking to ill-conditioned gradient eigenspectra, where slow modes lag behind fast memorization modes.

Theoretical clarity in a solvable model: The analytical analysis of the toy linear model in Section 3 and Appendix A clearly formalizes how the plateau length scales inversely with the smallest eigenvalue ($\sim 1/(\eta \varepsilon)$) and how equalizing the singular values eliminates this delay.

Strong empirical acceleration: Experiments across standard grokking benchmarks (modular addition, modular multiplication, sparse parity) demonstrate that EGD drastically reduces or eliminates the generalization plateau.
Exploration of practical variants: The inclusion of Randomized SVD (RSVD) and Column Normalization provides valuable insights into wall-clock trade-offs and computational tractability.
weaknesses: Novelty of the update rule relative to prior work: Mapping a matrix $G$ to $U V^\top$ via $(G G^\top)^{-1/2} G$ is precisely the polar decomposition of the gradient matrix. While Section 4.3 appropriately cites Muon, Muon and related polar/Newton-Schulz optimizers already employ the exact same geometric projection ($G \mapsto U V^\top$). While applying this lens specifically to grokking is interesting, the core algorithmic update itself is not entirely novel.

Computational overhead and scalability: Even with randomized SVD (RSVD), computing low-rank SVDs per layer at each iteration incurs non-trivial computational overhead compared to first-order optimizers. Scalability to large transformer models remains a significant practical bottleneck.

Conceptual ambiguity of 'accelerated grokking': In many experiments (e.g., Figures 1, 2, and 6), test accuracy improves almost concurrently with training accuracy under EGD. It raises the question of whether EGD is truly accelerating the internal mechanism of grokking, or simply functioning as an isotropic preconditioner that circumvents the ill-conditioned dynamics necessary for the grokking phenomenon to manifest.

Inconsistencies in pseudo-code: In Algorithm 2, the algorithm constructs $P = U S^{-1} U^\top$ and multiplies by $G$, even though $P G = U V^\top$ analytically. Furthermore, Algorithm 3 returns only $(\hat{U}, \hat{S})$ in line 11, omitting $\hat{V}^\top$, yet Algorithm 2 expects $(U, S, V^\top)$.

strengths: Principled perspective on grokking: The paper provides a clear, intuitive explanation of delayed generalization through the lens of ill-conditioned gradient spectra and disparate dynamical speeds along singular directions.

Tractable theoretical warm-up: The solvable 2D toy model (both in the distribution shift case and the equi-distributional case in Appendix A.3) nicely demonstrates how eigenvalue ill-conditioning ($1/\varepsilon$) directly translates to the length of the generalization plateau, and how preconditioning cancels this delay.

Clean mathematical formulation and connections: The proposed Egalitarian Gradient Descent (EGD) maps the gradient $G$ to its polar factor $\tilde{G} = UV^\top$, equalizing singular values while preserving singular directions. The paper effectively links this formulation to natural gradient descent (whitened NGD), Grokfast, and Muon.

Comprehensive empirical investigation: The authors test on classic grokking benchmarks (modular arithmetic, sparse parity) and explore practical approximations such as Randomized SVD (RSVD) and column normalization, tracking both epoch count and GPU wall-clock time.
weaknesses: Relation to established polar/orthogonal update optimizers: The core transformation $\tilde{G} = UV^\top = (GG^\top)^{-1/2}G$ is mathematically the polar factor of the gradient matrix. While Section 4.3 discusses Muon (which computes the polar factor using Newton-Schulz iterations), the mathematical operation of projecting the gradient/update onto the orthogonal Stiefel manifold has prior precedence in optimization (e.g., spectral normalization, polar updates, Shampoo variants). The conceptual novelty of the update rule itself is therefore somewhat incremental.

Toy theory vs. deep network grokking mechanisms: In the toy model, the delay is essentially slow convergence along an ill-conditioned direction in quadratic least-squares. While this provides clean mathematical tractability, real-world grokking in deep networks typically involves non-linear representation transitions, weight norm growth under weight decay, and competition between memorizing and generalizing subcircuits, which are not captured by the linear toy setting.

Omission of the primary baseline from the main text: Grokfast (Lee et al., 2024) is the primary baseline for grokking acceleration, yet direct empirical comparisons against Grokfast are deferred to the Appendix (Tables 6 and 7) rather than featured prominently in Section 5 of the main paper.

Computational practicality and stability: Computing exact SVD at each batch/step has high per-iteration overhead (often 3x to 5x higher Time/Epoch as shown in Tables 2–4). Furthermore, Table 7 and Figure 14 show that exact SVD EGD can exhibit severe instability in transformer architectures, making the choice of truncation rank in RSVD a crucial and potentially sensitive hyperparameter.

strengths: Compelling empirical demonstration that gradient spectral equalization dramatically reduces or eliminates generalization delays across canonical grokking benchmarks, including modular addition, modular multiplication, and sparse parity.

Comprehensive appendix providing wall-clock comparisons, practical approximations using Randomized SVD (RSVD), experiments on MNIST and a 2-layer transformer, and tests under non-stationary label shuffling.
The 2D anisotropic toy model provides a clear, analytically tractable illustration of how ill-conditioned feature/gradient dynamics can induce long plateaus in test performance.
weaknesses: Conceptual conflation of classical ill-conditioning with grokking: In the 2D linear regression toy setup (Section 3), the plateau is simply the standard slow convergence of gradient descent along the minor axis of an ill-conditioned quadratic bowl. Preconditioning an ill-conditioned quadratic with the inverse covariance/Hessian is a standard textbook result, and equating this directly to representation-learning grokking in deep non-linear networks stretches the definition.

Missing empirical comparison to Muon: As acknowledged in Section 4.3, both EGD and Muon replace the gradient/momentum matrix with its polar/orthogonal factor (UV^T). Given that Muon has gained substantial traction and directly computes the same geometric update via Newton-Schulz iterations, the lack of an empirical comparison against Muon is a significant omission.

Tenuous conceptual link between EGD and Grokfast: Section 1 and Section 4.2 assert that EGD is a 'simplified version of Grokfast' that 'inherits the filtering inductive bias of Grokfast'. This connection is conceptually strained: Grokfast performs temporal low-pass filtering across optimization steps using an exponential moving average buffer, whereas EGD flattens the instantaneous spatial singular spectrum of weight matrices at a single step.

Lack of statistical error bars: Grokking is well-known to be sensitive to initialization and random seed choices. The learning curves in Figures 1, 2, 3, 9, 10, and 11 appear to show single runs without confidence intervals or standard error bounds across multiple random seeds.

Computational scaling and instability: Exact SVD incurs significant computational overhead (as reflected in the per-epoch time in Tables 2–4). Furthermore, when applied to a 2-layer transformer (Figure 14), exact EGD displays severe training instability and is outperformed by Grokfast in both convergence steps and wall-clock time (Table 7).

strengths: Clear conceptual motivation: The paper provides an intuitive connection between ill-conditioned gradient eigenspectra (disparity between fast and slow singular directions) and the prolonged test-accuracy plateaus characteristic of grokking.

Analytically tractable toy model: The two-dimensional linear regression setup in Section 3 and the derivation in Theorem 1 and Corollary 1 offer clean, closed-form insights into how feature conditioning modulates plateau duration under gradient descent.

Simplicity of the core update: The proposed EGD transformation (replacing the gradient matrix G with its polar / semi-orthogonal factor UV^T) is mathematically clean, hyperparameter-free, and straightforward to implement.
weaknesses: Missing key empirical baseline (Grokfast): Section 4.2 dedicates substantial discussion to comparing EGD against Grokfast (Lee et al., 2024), highlighting advantages in memory, tuning, and theoretical backing. However, Grokfast is entirely absent from the empirical benchmarks (Figures 1, 2, and 3), leaving the claimed advantages untested against the primary literature baseline.

Overstated theoretical claims: The introduction and Section 4 claim that EGD is provably guaranteed to rapidly grok. However, the theoretical analysis is strictly confined to a 2D linear least-squares model under Gaussian/orthant assumptions. No convergence or grokking acceleration guarantees are established for multilayer neural networks or nonlinear architectures.

Limited architectural and experimental scope: Grokking in modular arithmetic is predominantly studied in small Transformers with AdamW, whereas the experiments here are restricted to two-layer MLPs compared only against vanilla SGD and a basic column-normalization heuristic. Evaluating Transformers and comparing with standard optimizers (e.g., AdamW, Muon, or sign-based methods) is necessary to demonstrate generality.

Disconnect between theory and deep network implementation: In Section 3, the preconditioning matrix is the inverse empirical data covariance. In Section 4, the transformation computes (GG^T)^{-1/2}G for a weight gradient matrix G in R^{m x p}. Equating GG^T to the layer Fisher Information Matrix ignores the full Kronecker-product structure of matrix parameter gradients (where the true empirical Fisher is an mp x mp matrix).

Computational overhead and lack of runtime analysis: Computing an SVD of the gradient matrix at every iteration adds non-trivial computational cost. While the paper suggests randomized SVD and switching to SGD after grokking as future/practical considerations, no wall-clock time comparisons or overhead measurements are reported.

strengths: The paper addresses an active and intriguing topic in deep learning dynamics: understanding and accelerating delayed generalization (grokking).

The proposed method, Egalitarian Gradient Descent (EGD), has an intuitive geometric motivation: replacing the singular values of the layer gradient matrix with 1 (taking $U V^\top$) to ensure uniform step scales across all principal directions.

The manuscript provides clear visualizations on synthetic algorithmic tasks (sparse parity and modular arithmetic) demonstrating that the modified update significantly reduces training epochs until generalization.
weaknesses: Missing critical baselines: Despite dedicating Section 4.2 entirely to comparing EGD conceptually with Grokfast (Lee et al., 2024) as the premier method for accelerating grokking, Grokfast is completely omitted from the empirical benchmarks in Figures 1, 2, and 3. Furthermore, standard optimizers such as AdamW (the standard optimizer under which grokking is typically studied), SGD with momentum, or matrix-orthogonalization methods (e.g., Muon / Shampoo) are not compared against. Vanilla SGD is an artificially weak baseline for modular arithmetic.

Conceptual and technical flaws in the connection to Natural Gradient Descent (Section 4.1): Defining the layer's empirical Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) as $F = G G^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times m}$ for a gradient matrix $G \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times p}$ is incorrect. The FIM is defined on the vectorized parameter space $\mathbb{R}^{mp \times mp}$ (or via Kronecker factors in K-FAC), not by simply multiplying the batch gradient matrix by its transpose. Moreover, the algebraic calculation on page 7 claiming $\frac{1}{m}\text{tr}[\tilde{G}^\top F \tilde{G}] = \frac{1}{m}\text{tr}(I)$ contains severe errors and confused notation.

Disconnection between the toy model and true grokking: The analytical model in Section 3 is simply an ill-conditioned 2-dimensional linear regression problem where convergence along the low-variance feature takes $O(1/\epsilon)$ steps. Calling the standard slow convergence of gradient descent on ill-conditioned quadratic objectives 'grokking' conflates basic linear optimization dynamics with the rich, non-linear representation-learning phenomena (e.g., competition between memorization and generalization circuits, kernel-to-rich transitions) that define grokking in the literature.

Unacknowledged prior art on polar-factor gradient updates: Transforming a 2D weight gradient $G = U S V^\top$ into $\tilde{G} = U V^\top$ is the polar decomposition / matrix orthogonalization step widely used in recent optimizers (such as Muon and Shampoo variants). The paper presents this update without contextualizing it within the extensive literature on orthogonalized/whitened matrix gradient methods.

Narrow experimental setup and lack of rigor: The evaluation is restricted to tiny two-layer MLPs on algorithmic datasets (modular arithmetic and sparse parity). There are no wall-clock time comparisons (which is critical because exact per-step SVD incurs non-trivial computational overhead), no standard deep learning benchmarks (e.g., transformers, vision models), and no reported error bars across multiple random seeds.

strengths: The core idea is simple, intuitive, and easy to understand: modifying the gradient by equalizing its singular values (i.e., replacing $G = U S V^\top$ with $\tilde{G} = U V^\top$) to prevent optimization from stalling along poorly conditioned directions.

The 2D toy model in Section 3 provides an exact analytic calculation showing how feature anisotropy and large initialization can create an optimization delay in test error for vanilla gradient descent.
The empirical results on modular arithmetic and sparse parity with two-layer MLPs show dramatic reduction in the number of epochs required to reach high test generalization compared to vanilla SGD.
weaknesses: Conceptual conflation of grokking with optimization ill-conditioning: The paper frames grokking as primarily arising from ill-conditioned gradient eigenspectra and slow optimization modes. In the literature, grokking specifically denotes delayed generalization where training error reaches zero early and remains flat for a long plateau before representation learning / implicit regularization drives generalization. In the toy linear model (Section 3), the delay is simply the classic convergence slowdown of gradient descent on ill-conditioned quadratics ($O(1/\varepsilon)$ steps), rather than the formation and competition of distinct circuits or escape from kernel regimes typical of grokking in deep networks.

Technical error in Section 4.1: The derivation showing that the Fisher-norm is a constant of motion is mathematically incorrect. Given $\tilde{G} = (GG^\top)^{-1/2} G$ and $F = GG^\top$, the transpose is $\tilde{G}^\top = G^\top (GG^\top)^{-1/2}$. Thus, $\tilde{G}^\top F \tilde{G} = G^\top (GG^\top)^{-1/2} (GG^\top) (GG^\top)^{-1/2} G = G^\top G$, whose trace is $\text{tr}(G^\top G) = \sum_j s_j^2 \neq \text{tr}(I)$. Furthermore, calling $F = GG^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times m}$ the empirical Fisher Information Matrix of a layer with weight matrix $W \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times p}$ is inaccurate, as the true Fisher matrix is of size $(mp) \times (mp)$ defined over expectations of sample-wise score outer products.

Missing primary baseline in experimental evaluation: The paper dedicates significant discussion (Section 2 and Section 4.2) to Grokfast (Lee et al., 2024), highlighting theoretical and conceptual distinctions. However, Grokfast is completely absent from all experimental figures (Figures 1, 2, and 3). Without empirical comparison against Grokfast or other acceleration baselines (e.g., AdamW with weight decay, Grokalign), it is impossible to assess whether EGD provides any practical advantage over existing techniques.

Narrow experimental evaluation and computational overhead: Experiments are restricted strictly to 2-layer MLPs on synthetic arithmetic and parity problems. Most seminal studies on grokking (Power et al., 2022; Zhong et al., 2023; Nanda et al., 2023) focus on Transformer architectures. Moreover, performing SVD on layer gradients at every iteration incurs significant computational overhead ($O(m p \min(m, p))$), but the paper provides no wall-clock time comparisons or scaling analysis.

Unaddressed connections to orthogonalized gradient methods: The update $\tilde{G} = UV^\top$ corresponds to the unitary factor in the polar decomposition of the matrix gradient. This transformation has deep connections to preconditioned/orthogonalized optimization (e.g., Shampoo, polar gradient descent, Muon), which the manuscript overlooks entirely.
